title: Prepare for the showing and help the buyer decide

slides.title: Prepare for a successful showing
slides.lead: Day 3 · 74 minutes including discussion and practice
slides.body: Help the buyer understand what works, what does not, and what to do next.
slides.theme: tru alms alms-cover training-depth
slides.notes:
Today we are going to work on the first showing. Success is not whether they buy the house we open. Success is whether we understand them better and they leave knowing how we will help them move forward. Introduce yourself and connect today to the first-call work in Day 2.

Sources: INT-005–007; Eric’s Day 3 objective. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.

slides.title: What should be ready before tomorrow’s showing?
slides.lead: You are meeting a buyer tomorrow. They want a quiet office and a usable yard. They have an afternoon available for the tour.
slides.body:
1. What would you research about each home?
  2. How many homes would you propose, and why?
  3. What would you ask the listing agent and confirm with the buyer?
After your answer: review the explanation
Prepare two to four relevant homes when the buyer’s time, preferences and access allow. Review available property information and comparisons, call the listing agent, explain tradeoffs, confirm access and bring a useful packet. The number supports a thoughtful tour; it does not override the buyer’s needs.

slides.title: Review the property information before the showing
slides.lead: Know what the available records say and which questions remain unanswered.
slides.body:
Read the available documents

Review the listing and seller disclosures. Identify facts that affect the buyer’s stated needs and flag missing information.

Prepare useful comparisons

Review three relevant comparable sales where available. Note the differences that make each comparison useful rather than assuming the prices are directly interchangeable.

Check practical details

Review property taxes and school district information. Record the source and any question that needs confirmation. Explain the information without guessing.

slides.title: Call the listing agent with specific questions
slides.lead: Use the call to prepare accurate information and confirm the visit.
slides.body:
Ask about the listing

“Is there an offer deadline or offer activity we should know about?” Ask about seller timing and any rent-back request.

Ask about unresolved facts

“The available materials do not state the roof age. Is there documentation you can share?” Keep reported information separate from verified documents.

Confirm access

Check appointment approval and showing instructions. A buyer’s preferred time does not establish access. If an answer is pending, record it and plan the update.

slides.title: Choose two to four homes for a useful comparison
slides.lead: Use the buyer’s priorities, available time and confirmed access to shape the tour.
slides.body:
Explain why each home belongs

“This home has the enclosed office you wanted. The yard is smaller. Would comparing the layout still be useful?”

Respect firm requirements

If the yard is nonnegotiable, revise the options. More homes are useful only when the comparisons help the buyer decide.

Confirm the tour plan

Agree on the meeting place, sequence and timing. Review access instructions and the applicable brokerage-approved agreement before the visit.

slides.title: Bring information the buyer can use during the tour
slides.lead: Print a buyer copy for each home. Keep your research notes with you so you can answer questions during the tour.
slides.body:
Documents for the buyer

Use the customer-facing report from your MLS. Check the address, current status, price and report date. Include relevant comparable sales and identify the source and date of any neighborhood information.

Notes for you

Highlight features the buyer asked for. List unanswered questions, who you have asked, and when you will follow up. Keep agent-only remarks and access instructions out of the buyer’s packet.

Before leaving

Confirm every appointment, check showing instructions, and send the buyer the meeting address and time. Bring the printed packet and your notes.

A complete plan connects each home to the buyer’s needs, identifies missing property information, confirms access and timing, and includes useful documents. Explain any tradeoff before the visit. Adjust the selection when a firm requirement is not met.

slides.title: Make it safe to dislike the home
slides.lead: Tell buyers at the start that honest feedback helps you choose homes for them.
slides.body: “Take your time looking around. Tell me what you like and what doesn’t work for you—you won’t hurt my feelings. That helps me narrow down what we look at next.”

slides.title: Let them experience the home
slides.lead: Let buyers look around and talk to each other before you ask for their reaction.
slides.body:
Give them room

Stay nearby so they can ask questions. Let them finish looking through a room before you speak; a quiet moment does not need to be filled.

Follow what they say

If they say the office feels small, ask: “What would you need to fit in here?” Listen before suggesting another use for the room.

Say when you do not know

“I don’t have the roof replacement date. I’ll ask the listing agent for documentation and update you by five.” Record the question and send the update even if the answer is still pending.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson day3-polish lesson-photo photo-conversation training-depth

slides.cue: Next: Let the buyer’s reaction lead to one useful question. Connect it to the action you just practiced.

slides.title: Let the buyer’s reaction lead to one useful question
slides.lead: Give them time to experience the room. When they share a reaction, follow that thought instead of starting a list of questions.
slides.body:
Buyer
“This office could work.”

Let them look around and finish their thought.

Agent
“What would work better here than in your current setup?”

Ask one question tied to what they just said. Then listen.

Buyer
“I could close the door during calls.”

Now you know why the room matters. Check your understanding before changing the search.

“So you need a room where you can close the door for calls. Is that right?”
slides.theme: tru alms lesson day3-polish training-depth conversation-example
slides.notes:
Give agents this as a working question bank, not a checklist. Model asking one question, listening, and building the next question from the answer. “A bigger house” becomes useful when we learn why the current space fails. A summary is a check with the buyer, not an agent deciding their priorities for them.

Sources: R005; R021; INT-005–007,038. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.

slides.title: What would you ask before the buyer leaves?
slides.lead: The tour has finished. The buyer has mentioned things they liked and things that did not work.
slides.body:
1. How would you ask for a few minutes?
  2. What would your first question be?
  3. What changes if they say yes, no or unsure?
After your answer: review the explanation
Ask for a few minutes and explain the purpose. Start with “Did we see any homes we want to write an offer on?” Then follow the answer. Do not infer a decision from silence, criticism or a rating.

slides.title: Take five minutes to review the tour and ask about an offer
slides.lead: Before everyone leaves the last home, ask the buyers to stay for a short conversation.
slides.body:
Invite the conversation
“We’ve looked at several houses today. Before we wrap up, I like to take five minutes with my clients to talk through what we saw. Do you have a few minutes now?”

If you toured one home, say “this house.” If they need to leave, agree on a specific time to talk.

Ask the first question
“Did we see any homes we want to write an offer on?”

Pause and let them answer. Give each buyer time to speak before you recommend a next step.

Use their answer to choose your next question: which home, what did not work, or what they still need to know.

slides.title: Let the offer answer guide your next question
slides.lead: Ask the follow-up that matches their answer. You do not need to ask every question on this slide.
slides.body:
Yes: identify the home and questions

“Which home would you like to make an offer on? Is there anything you need answered before we talk through the offer?” Write down those questions and arrange the offer conversation.

No: find out what to change

“Which home came closest? What was missing?” If comparing homes is difficult, ask for a one-to-ten rating and what would raise it. Confirm which search criteria to change.

Unsure: name what is holding them back

“What are you still thinking through?” Listen first. Then ask what information would help them decide and agree who will get it and when you will talk again.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: Reasons buyers may hesitate after a showing
slides.lead: These statements begin a conversation. Learn what is behind them before deciding how to help.
slides.body:
• “We would rather keep renting.”
  • “We are about six months out.”
  • “I am unsure about interest rates.”
  • “I do not know what payment we can afford.”
  • “We may need to relocate for work.”
  • “We need to sell our current home first.”
slides.theme: tru alms lesson day3-polish training-depth
slides.notes:
Read a few examples and ask what else agents have heard. Keep this as one overview, not six objection scripts. Some statements describe a real need or a firm constraint. Six months might be a lease, a work decision, preparation they need, or simply an estimate. We do not know until we ask. The objective is to build a plan for when it is right for this buyer, not convince them to buy today.

Sources: Eric’s current correction; R006, R020, R024; INT-045–050. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.
Handoff: Next: What would you ask to understand the buyer?. Connect it to the action you just practiced.
slides.cue: Next: What would you ask to understand the buyer?. Connect it to the action you just practiced.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: What would you ask to understand the buyer?
slides.lead: Choose a statement from the list below. Explain what you would ask, what you might learn, and how that would change the plan.
slides.body:
• “We would rather keep renting.”
  • “We are about six months out.”
  • “I am unsure about interest rates.”
Compare with the teaching example
Start by understanding the reason. A firm six-month constraint calls for a preparation plan around that date; an uncertain payment may call for an agreed lender conversation to explore options. Neither answer means the buyer must purchase now. Explain why your suggested help matters, ask whether it would be useful, and agree on actions and the next contact.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson day3-polish lesson-question training-depth
slides.notes:
Let the room choose which concern to explore rather than assigning a rebuttal to each one. Give thirty seconds to write an acknowledgment and question. Invite someone to play the buyer and answer it. Ask another agent to propose help based on that answer. Then change the buyer’s reason and ask how the plan changes. For six months, contrast a firm work-related constraint with an estimate based on uncertainty about payment. Ask: What can we help them prepare now? What should wait? For rates, learn what the uncertainty means before offering lender input. The test is whether the recommendation serves the buyer’s actual need, not whether they agree to buy sooner.

Sources: Eric’s current correction; R006, R020, R024; INT-045–050. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: Understand the concern before proposing a solution
slides.lead: Ask what the buyer means before suggesting a lender call, another tour or a different timeline.
slides.body:
Repeat the concern in their words

If they say they want to wait six months: “Okay, you’re thinking about six months from now.” Avoid telling them you understand a reason they have not explained.

Ask about the reason

“What’s happening in six months?” Let them answer. A lease ending, a work move and saving for a down payment call for different plans.

Offer one step that addresses the answer

For a payment question, offer a lender conversation. For a home they must sell first, offer to discuss the sale timeline. Ask whether that would help, then agree on an action and a follow-up time.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: Connect the next step to the buyer’s goal
slides.lead: Fictional example: the buyer wants to move before their lease ends in six months, but is unsure what interest rates would mean for their payment.
slides.body:
“Your lease ends in six months, and you want to know what the monthly payment would be before you decide. Would you like me to introduce you to a lender to go through the numbers? Or do you already have someone you’d like to call?”

If they want the introduction

Confirm how and when they want to connect. After the lender call is scheduled, ask: “When would be a good time for us to talk through what you learned?” Save that follow-up.

If they decline

“Okay. What would you like to do from here?” Listen and agree on whether and when they want you to contact them again.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: Update the buyer when a property answer is still pending
slides.lead: After a showing, a buyer says they may want to make an offer, but need the roof age first. You promised an update by 5. It is 4:45, and the listing agent has not replied. What would you do next?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example
B fits the uncertainty. Keep the buyer informed before five, clarify how the answer affects their decision, and seek team-lead advice if it is urgent. Propose a next update you control. Do not guarantee a third-party answer. A may become appropriate after agreement and understanding urgency; C assumes enough information to set an offer plan.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson day3-polish lesson-question training-depth
slides.notes:
Ask for a choice and the information that could change it. Discuss the difference between “I may want to offer” and “I need this now to decide on an offer.” Ask: What can you commit to when you cannot control the listing agent? What should the buyer hear by five? Have an agent speak the update. Reveal the example after the room has worked through the tradeoff.

Sources: R025; INT-051. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: Confirm the action and the next contact before you leave
slides.lead: Summarize the agreement out loud, then ask whether it works for the buyer.
slides.body:
Say what you will do

“I’ll ask the listing agent for the roof documentation.” Name the action instead of saying you will look into things.

Confirm what the buyer agreed to do

Only include actions they accepted. If they agreed to contact their lender, confirm what they want to ask and when they expect to have the conversation.

Set the next contact

“I’ll call you by five today, even if I’m still waiting for the document. Does that work for you?” Save a task for the time you agreed on.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: Save what changed and what you promised
slides.lead: Before your next appointment, save the conversation and follow-up in Follow Up Boss.
slides.body:
Write the note

Record the homes discussed, what the buyer liked or ruled out, and why. Add unanswered questions, promised actions and the agreed contact time. Do not record an assumption as a buyer decision.

Update the stage

Use Met with customer after the first appointment; Showing homes after the second.

Create the task

Assign yourself the promised action with a due date and time. A note alone will not remind you to call. Send the update on time even if you are still waiting for someone else.

slides.chapter: 4. Understand concerns and agree on a plan
slides.title: Practice the showing and agree on a plan
slides.lead: Work in pairs or trios. Everyone takes an agent turn and responds to what the buyer actually says.
slides.body:
Set up · 1 minute

Choose the assigned buyer card. Use the meeting platform for breakout rooms.

Three rounds · 4 minutes each

Agent: welcome and discovery for 2 minutes. Observer: one specific correction for 1 minute. Agent: retry for 1 minute. Rotate roles.

Debrief · 3 minutes

What answer changed your plan? What did your partner improve on the retry?

Compare with the teaching example
Look for a welcome that invites honest reactions, a follow-up that uses the buyer’s answer, and a specific agreed plan. Feedback names an observed moment; the retry improves that moment. A decision to wait can be sound when the plan fits the reason.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson day3-polish lesson-photo photo-practice training-depth lesson-question
slides.notes:
Use rotating trios with agent, buyer, and observer, or pairs where the buyer gives feedback. In pairs, both take an agent turn and use the third round to retry the harder moment. In each turn briefly welcome the buyer, then move to the end of the fictional tour and build a plan from the card. Buyer: supply the card facts naturally when asked, and do not agree automatically. Observer: name one actual moment and one correction. Do not label a peer or self-check as coach sign-off. Submit the buyer answer and plan after the conversation, not before the buyer has spoken. If testing solo, set up solo speaking practice and record test observations. A solo run cannot verify a live peer’s performance.

Sources: R005–006; R020–025; INT-005–007,035–039,048–051. Buyer examples are fictional teaching scenarios adapted from Eric’s process.

Partner check: Is the plan based on what the buyer said? Can someone tell who does what and when?

Compare with the teaching example
The note reflects the conversation, separates unknowns from facts, and records the agreed action. The stage matches the completed appointment. The task supports a useful next contact at the agreed time or trigger.

Give a minute to write and submit. Read two contrasting plans with permission. Ask the room what each next contact will accomplish. Correct invented facts, missing agreement, or a generic “checking in.” Have the agent revise that part. This is a written practice record, not a change to a real FUB contact. Review the real submitted answers in the presenter panel.

slides.title: Your next showing should end with a plan
slides.lead: Use these steps on your next tour, then save the agreement in Follow Up Boss.
slides.body:
Before the tour

Research the selected homes, list unanswered questions and confirm access, timing and your buyer packet.

During the tour

Let buyers look around. Listen to their reactions and ask a follow-up about what matters to them.

Before leaving

Ask about an offer. Follow their answer, agree on who will do what and when, then save the note and follow-up task.

slides.lead: Revisit the explanation, try the exercise, then compare your work.
slides.body:
Find the topic

Use the four sections to return to the action you need. Read the example and the reason for the next step.

Practice again

Answer the scenario before opening its explanation. For a conversation exercise, use the buyer card with a partner, get one specific correction, and retry.

Keep a reference

Download the agent reference for the teaching and examples. Keep practice notes separate from real customer records.

cases.name: Case 1 · The home does not fit
cases.quote: “We liked the living area, but I could hear everything from the office. We are still figuring out what matters.”
cases.goal: Buyer facts: one buyer takes work calls at home; a quiet enclosed office matters more than an extra bedroom. They want to compare two quieter layouts next Saturday if access works. Reveal the reason when asked. Agent: learn what “quiet” requires and agree on a search and confirmation plan; do not promise access.

cases.name: Case 2 · The timing has a reason
cases.quote: “We like the home, but we keep saying a year. I do not know what payment we would be comfortable with.”
cases.goal: Buyer facts: a year is an estimate, not a fixed deadline. They have not spoken to a lender and want information before deciding whether buying fits. They are open to an introduction, not committed to buying. Agent: clarify the concern, offer relevant preparation, and agree how to reconnect without accelerating their decision.

cases.name: Case 3 · An answer is holding up the decision
cases.quote: “This one could work, but the roof worries me. I need to understand that before deciding whether to take the next step.”
cases.goal: Buyer facts: the roof age is unknown. They would like to consider an offer soon if they can understand the issue, but have not decided to offer. They can talk again at six. Agent: establish what information matters and how urgent it is, seek appropriate help, and agree on an update without promising the outside answer.

resources: Use the question bank and buyer cards to practice again. In a live session, submit your responses through your learner screen. The printed worksheet does not submit answers. Keep practice evidence separate from observed work with an actual client.
